title: Smaller than small, greater than great (3.20)
hook: the Upanishad describes the self as tinier than an atom and vaster than the sky, in the same breath
tomorrow: Bhakti — the first use of the word in the Upanishads

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rudra, the storm and the healer, the one who rules all the worlds with no second. Did you find both storm and healer somewhere in your day? Today ends the week. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

Anor aniyan mahato mahiyan. Two pictures that refuse to sit still together. Smaller than a grain of sand, smaller than a cell, smaller than anything a microscope can show. And at the same time bigger than the earth, bigger than the sky, bigger than every star. Try to hold both, and the mind tends to flip from one to the other like a coin. That flip is what today's verse is after. It sets the two pictures side by side and says: this is what the self is like.
screen: `SMALLER THAN A GRAIN OF SAND.` → `BIGGER THAN THE SKY.` → `HOLD BOTH AT ONCE?`

segments.voice: Verse 3.20, in paraphrase: smaller than the small, greater than the great, the self is hidden in the heart of every creature. Free of craving, free of sorrow, one sees that Lord and his greatness through the grace of the creator. Those opening words, anor aniyan mahato mahiyan, also appear in the Katha Upanishad, in a nearly identical verse. The difference is at the end. In the Katha, the last phrase is usually read as seeing the self through the calm of the senses. In the Shvetashvatara, almost the same sounds are read as through the grace of the creator. A tiny shift, and the whole verse tilts toward a personal God who gives. Why say both small and great? Because any single picture would be a cage. Call it small, and you put it in a box. Call it great, and you make it far away. Say both, and the mind can't settle on either, and has to let go. This week has been full of that letting go. Day one asked what the cause is: time, nature, chance? Day two counted the wheel. Day three set the swan circling it. Day four churned the fire sticks. Day five sat up straight. Day six named Rudra, one with no second. And today, a paradox: the same reality hidden in your heart and spread past the stars.
screen: `SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.` · `THE KATHA SAYS IT TOO.` · `ONE PICTURE WOULD BE A CAGE.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `IN THE HEART, BEYOND THE STARS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring your attention to a single point at the center of your chest, as small as you can make it, a pinprick. Stay there for a few breaths. Then let your attention widen, past your body, past the room, past the town, out to the sky. Stay there for a few breaths. Then go back to the point. Small, then vast. Let the two pictures trade places, and notice what stays the same while they change. The bell holds the time.
Smaller than small. The first half of the Upanishad's paradox: the self, finer than an atom, hidden in the heart, and also greater than the greatest.
Your line: the paradox. Once today, look at something tiny, a seed, a drop, an ant, and then at the sky, and say quietly: smaller than small, greater than great. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Hindus chant anor aniyan mahato mahiyan as part of Upanishad recitation, and Vedanta teachers often use it to show that the self cannot be pictured by size at all.

fork.setup: a student asks the teacher: is the self small or great? what does verse 3.20 answer?
options: small: it lives in the heart.
both at once, so that no single picture can hold it.
fork.reveal: smaller than the small, greater than the great. the paradox keeps the mind from boxing the self into any one image.

original.note: Sanskrit aṇor aṇīyān: smaller than the small. paired with mahato mahīyān, greater than the great.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic way of saying 'everywhere'.
what it means: the self can't be measured by size: it is in the heart of each being and beyond everything.

what a scholar hears: Katha 1.2.20 and Shvetashvatara 3.20 share the line, but the ending is read differently: dhatu-prasada (calm of the senses) in the Katha, dhatuh prasada (the creator's grace) in the Shvetashvatara.
